mainTopic: Oaths by descriptions of ה׳, which written names are holy or may be erased, and whether a כנוי is enough for a שבועת העדות
overview: The גמרא finishes אביי's explanation that an oath 'by the Gracious and Compassionate' counts as an oath by ה׳, since only ה׳ fits those words. Heaven and earth are different, because they really exist on their own. Next, ברייתות teach which partial names of ה׳ may be erased. They also teach whether letters added before or after a name may be erased, and the הלכה follows אחרים that endings after the name may not be erased. Then the גמרא goes through פסוקים in the stories of אברהם, לוט, נבות, מיכה, גבעת בנימין, שיר השירים and דניאל, asking whether each name is holy (קודש) or ordinary (חול). Along the way it learns that welcoming guests is greater than greeting the שכינה, and it rereads the יש אומרים so that שמואל's teaching has a source. Finally, it returns to the משנה's rule that an oath with a כנוי makes witnesses liable. אביי answers a ברייתא that seems to require ה׳'s actual name: the two sources follow different תנאים. The גמרא then explains how the רבנן know that the witnesses' אלה includes an oath without requiring the actual Name.

steps.title: Finishing the answer: the oath means the Compassionate One
steps.stepSummary: The end of אביי's answer: when the משנה speaks of an oath 'by the Compassionate,' it means 'by the One Who is compassionate,' which is ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה means: 'by the One Who is compassionate.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes an answer that started earlier. אביי explained that an oath 'by the Gracious and Compassionate' is really an oath by ה׳, the One Who has those traits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Gracious' and 'compassionate' are not names of ה׳ by themselves. Still, אביי says the person is pointing to ה׳ through those descriptions, so the oath counts as a real oath by ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: by the One Who is (pointing to ה׳ through a description)
he is saying / the תנא is speaking about

phrases.english: "By the One Who is compassionate" is what he is saying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's answer from the previous part of the daf.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Gracious and compassionate' are not names of ה׳, so an oath by them should not count.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words describe ה׳, so the oath counts as an oath by ה׳.

steps.title: Then heaven and earth should count too
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי: by the same logic, an oath 'by heaven and earth' should mean 'by the One Who owns heaven and earth' and should also count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If so, an oath 'by heaven and by earth' should also be read as 'by the One to Whom heaven and earth belong'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's answer. If a description can point to ה׳, why does the משנה exempt an oath by heaven and earth?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats 'by heaven and earth' as a non-oath. רבא argues that אביי's method would turn that into an oath by ה׳ too, which contradicts the משנה.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If so, "by heaven and by earth" too –
he should be saying "by the One to Whom heaven and earth belong"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning of step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading of 'gracious and compassionate' as pointing to ה׳
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If descriptions point to ה׳, 'heaven and earth' should also point to their Owner, yet the משנה exempts that oath.

steps.title: Why heaven and earth are different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison: nothing besides ה׳ is called gracious and compassionate, but heaven and earth are real things, so the person may mean them literally.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, since nothing else is called compassionate and gracious, he surely means 'by the One Who is gracious' and 'by the One Who is compassionate.' Here, since heaven and earth really exist, he means heaven and earth themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אביי and shows the two cases are not the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A description that fits only ה׳ must point to ה׳. Heaven and earth exist on their own, so swearing by them most likely means the actual sky and ground, not their Creator. That is why the משנה exempts this oath.

keyTerms.meaning: how can you compare? (rejects a comparison)

steps.whatToRemember: An oath by a description counts as an oath by ה׳ only when the description can fit no one but ה׳. 'Heaven and earth' are real things, so that oath is not by ה׳.

phrases.english: How can you compare?!
There, since there is nothing else
that is called compassionate and gracious –
certainly "by the One Who is gracious,"
certainly "by the One Who is compassionate" is what he says.
Here, since there are a heaven and an earth –
"by heaven and by earth" is what he says.
phrases.notes: He means the actual sky and ground, not their Owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any description, including heaven and earth, could point to ה׳.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a description that fits ה׳ alone points to ה׳; heaven and earth are taken literally.

steps.title: Which partial divine names may be erased
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that writing אל from אלהים or יה from the four-letter name may not be erased, but שד from שדי, אד from אדני, or צב from צבאות may be erased.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: If someone wrote אל from 'אלהים' or 'יה' from the four-letter name, it may not be erased. If he wrote שד from 'שדי', אד from 'אדני', or צב from 'צבאות', it may be erased.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about the holiness of written names of ה׳, specifically when only the first two letters were written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some two-letter beginnings are themselves names of ה׳‎ (אל and יה), so they keep their holiness and may not be erased. Other two-letter beginnings (שד, אד, צב) are not names by themselves, so they may be erased.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying that שדי, אדני, or צבאות may be erased. It is only talking about their first two letters written alone.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule for a סופר who began writing a name of ה׳ and stopped partway.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If one wrote alef-lamed from "אלהים,"
or yod-heh from the four-letter name –
phrases.notes: The four-letter name is written here as יְיָ, a common way to avoid writing it out.

phrases.english: this may not be erased.
Shin-dalet from "שדי,"
alef-dalet from "אדני,"
tzadi-beit from "צבאות" –
this may be erased.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כָּתַב אָלֶף לָמֶד מֵאֱלֹהִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the oath discussion to a new ברייתא about erasing names of ה׳.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אל from אלהים and יה from the four-letter name may not be erased; שד, אד, and צב may be erased.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: צבאות may be fully erased
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says the whole word צבאות may be erased, because it refers to the Jewish people and is not one of ה׳'s own names.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says the whole word צבאות may be erased. ה׳ is called צבאות only because of the Jewish people, as the פסוק says, "I will bring out My hosts, My people the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now brings רבי יוסי, who disagrees with the earlier rule about צבאות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 4 only part of the word, צב, could be erased, which means the full word צבאות counts as a holy name. רבי יוסי says the full word may also be erased. He points to the פסוק where צבאות means the Jewish people, ה׳'s 'hosts.' So in his view it is a description and not a true name of ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: Hosts; a title used with ה׳'s name

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says: 'Tzevaot' may be erased in its entirety,
because He is called 'Tzevaot'
only because of Israel,
as it says: 'And I will bring out My hosts,
phrases.notes: שמות 7:4

phrases.aramaic: אֶת עַמִּי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם״.
phrases.english: My people the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disagreeing opinion inside the same ברייתא, about the word צבאות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In רבי יוסי's view, the full word צבאות may be erased because it is not a name of ה׳.

steps.title: שמואל rules against רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says the הלכה does not follow רבי יוסי, so צבאות is treated as a holy name.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives the practical ruling on the disagreement about צבאות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי, we follow the first opinion. The full word צבאות may not be erased, and only part of it, such as צב, may be erased.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law is not like this opinion

steps.whatToRemember: In practice, צבאות is a holy name and may not be erased.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי.
phrases.english: Shmuel said: The halakha is not like Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the disagreement from Step 5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה is not like רבי יוסי, so the full word צבאות may not be erased.

steps.title: Letters attached before ה׳'s name may be erased
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that extra letters attached to ה׳'s name may be erased, and lists the letters that can come before it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: any letters attached to ה׳'s name, whether before it or after it, may be erased. Before it, how? In 'to ה׳,' the ל may be erased. The same is true of the ב ('in'), the ו ('and'), the מ ('from'), the ש ('that'), the ה (asking 'is it?'), and the כ ('like').
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא states a general rule: added letters are not holy. It then gives examples of letters that come before the name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hebrew often joins small words like 'to,' 'in,' or 'and' onto the front of a word as one letter. The ברייתא says these letters are not part of the holy name. So one may erase just that letter and leave the name itself.

keyTerms.meaning: What is attached to the name but is not part of it
In front of it, a letter added before the word

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: Anything attached to the name,
whether before it or after it,
may be erased.
Before it, how so?
'To ה׳': the lamed may be erased;
'In ה׳': the beit may be erased;
'And ה׳': the vav may be erased;
'From ה׳': the mem may be erased;
'That ה׳': the shin may be erased;
'Is it ה׳?': the heh may be erased;
'Like ה׳': the kaf may be erased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from parts of names inside a word to extra letters added onto the name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Letters added in front of ה׳'s name are not holy and may be erased.

steps.title: Letters attached after ה׳'s name may be erased
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives examples of endings added after ה׳'s name, which according to this opinion may also be erased.
steps.simpleTranslation: After it, how? In 'our God,' the ending נו may be erased. In 'their God,' the ending הם may be erased. In 'your God,' the ending כם may be erased.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the second half of its rule: endings that come after the name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Endings such as 'our,' 'their,' and 'your' are joined to אלהים at the end of the word. The first opinion treats them just like letters added in front: they are not part of the name and may be erased. This sets up the disagreement that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: After it, a letter or ending added after the name

phrases.english: After it, how so?
'Eloheinu' (our God): the nu may be erased,
'Eloheihem' (their God): the hem may be erased,
'Eloheichem' (your God): the chem may be erased.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's examples, moving from letters before the name to endings after it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the first opinion, endings after ה׳'s name may also be erased.

steps.title: אחרים: endings after the name may not be erased
steps.stepSummary: אחרים say endings after ה׳'s name may not be erased, because the name has already made them holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחרים say: what comes after the name may not be erased, because the name has already made it holy.
steps.whatsHappening: A different opinion, called אחרים, disagrees with the second half of the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אחרים agree about letters in front of the name, since they disagree only about 'after it.' Their reason is that once the name is written, an ending added to it takes on the name's holiness. Letters written before the name did not get this, because the name was not there yet when they were written.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Others'; a תנא quoted under this name

steps.confusionAlert: אחרים argue only about endings AFTER the name. Everyone agrees that letters BEFORE the name may be erased.

phrases.english: Acherim say: What is after it may not be erased,
because the name has already made it holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the rule in Step 8 about endings after the name.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Endings after ה׳'s name share its holiness and may not be erased.

steps.title: רב הונא rules like אחרים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that the הלכה follows אחרים, so endings after ה׳'s name may not be erased.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: the הלכה is like אחרים.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives the practical ruling on the disagreement about endings after the name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, letters before the name may be erased, but endings like נו, הם, and כם after אלהים may not. These endings are treated as part of the holy name.
steps.whatToRemember: Letters before ה׳'s name may be erased. Endings after the name may not be erased, because the הלכה follows אחרים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This matters in practice for anyone writing or correcting a ספר תורה or other holy writing.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said: The halakha is like Acherim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides between Step 8 and Step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Endings after ה׳'s name may not be erased.

steps.title: Memory list for the coming topics
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a list of memory words, one for each of the next topics.
steps.simpleTranslation: A memory list: אברהם, the one who cursed נבות, in גבעת בנימין, שלמה, דניאל.
steps.whatsHappening: This is not an argument. The גמרא is setting up the next sections with a list of memory hooks, one word for each coming topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word in the list points to a פסוק the גמרא will soon discuss. In each one, it will ask whether a word is a holy name of ה׳ or an ordinary word.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid for the topics that follow

phrases.english: (Abraham; who cursed Naboth;
phrases.notes: This is a memory list to help you remember what's coming, not part of the discussion itself. Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: in Gibeah of Benjamin; Solomon; Daniel: a memory aid)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the rules about added letters to a new list of topics that comes next.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A memory list for the coming discussions about which words in פסוקים are holy names.

steps.title: Names with אברהם are holy, except one
steps.stepSummary: Every name of ה׳ in the אברהם stories is קודש, except the אדני in 'אדני אם נא מצאתי חן', which is חול.
steps.simpleTranslation: All names in the Torah connected to אברהם are holy, except this one, which is ordinary: 'And he said: My lords, if I have found favor in your eyes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts the first topic on its memory list. It rules that in the אברהם stories every name is holy except one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When אברהם sees the three guests, he says 'אדני'. This opinion holds that he was talking to the guests (really מלאכים), so the word means 'my lords' and is חול. Everywhere else in אברהם's stories, the name means ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: Holy: the word refers to ה׳ and may not be erased
Ordinary: the word does not refer to ה׳
Can mean ה׳'s name, or 'my lords / my masters'

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל שֵׁמוֹת הָאֲמוּרִים בַּתּוֹרָה בְּאַבְרָהָם – קֹדֶשׁ;
phrases.english: All names stated in the Torah in connection with Avraham are holy;
except for this one, which is ordinary,
as it says: "And he said: My lords,
phrases.notes: בראשית 18:3. Here אברהם is speaking to his three guests.

phrases.english: if I have found favor in your eyes."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the first topic from the memory list in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the אברהם stories all names are קודש except 'אדני' in בראשית 18:3, which is חול.

steps.title: A pair of תנאים say that name is holy too
steps.stepSummary: חנינא בן אחי רבי יהושע and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, quoting רבי אלעזר המודעי, say the אדני in that פסוק is also קודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: חנינא, the son of רבי יהושע's brother, and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, in the name of רבי אלעזר המודעי, said: This one is also holy.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion disagrees with step 12. It says even the one exception is a holy name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this view, אברהם was not talking to the guests. He was speaking to ה׳, asking Him to wait while he took care of the guests. So the אדני there means ה׳ and is קודש.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of; quoting someone

phrases.english: Chanina, the son of Rabbi Yehoshua's brother,
and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
said in the name of Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i:
This one too is holy.
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the אדני from the פסוק just quoted, the one the first opinion called ordinary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the exception given in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The אדני in בראשית 18:3 is also קודש; אברהם was speaking to ה׳.

steps.title: Whose view supports welcoming guests over greeting the שכינה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which opinion fits רב's teaching that הכנסת אורחין is greater than greeting the שכינה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose opinion does this follow, what רב יהודה said in the name of רב: Welcoming guests is greater than greeting the שכינה. Whose opinion?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which of the two opinions it just quoted matches a famous teaching of רב. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's lesson comes from אברהם leaving ה׳ to run to his guests. That lesson only works if אברהם was speaking to ה׳ in that פסוק. So the גמרא wants to know which opinion reads it that way.

phrases.english: Whose opinion does this follow,
what Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav:
Welcoming guests is greater
than greeting the Divine Presence.
Whose opinion is it?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which side of the disagreement in steps 12 and 13 fits רב's teaching.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion about the אדני of אברהם supports רב's lesson about הכנסת אורחין?

steps.title: It follows that pair of תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רב's teaching follows the pair from step 13, who hold that אברהם was speaking to ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like that pair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question. רב's teaching matches the opinion of the pair of תנאים in step 13.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For that pair, אברהם asked ה׳ to wait so he could serve his guests. That shows that welcoming guests came before standing with the שכינה. According to the first opinion, אברהם was only talking to the guests, so there is no such lesson.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's famous lesson, גדולה הכנסת אורחין יותר מהקבלת פני שכינה, rests on reading אברהם's 'אדני' as ה׳'s name, which is the view of the pair in step 13.

phrases.english: Like that pair.
phrases.notes: He means חנינא and רבי אלעזר בן עזריה, the two who said 'this one too is holy.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב's teaching follows the pair of תנאים who say the אדני is קודש.

steps.title: Names with לוט are ordinary, except one
steps.stepSummary: In the לוט story every name is חול, except the אדני in 'אל נא אדני', which is קודש because לוט is speaking to the One Who can give life.
steps.simpleTranslation: All names connected to לוט are ordinary, except this one, which is holy: 'And לוט said to them: Please, not so, אדני; behold your servant has found favor in your eyes.' The One Who has the power to kill and to give life is הקדוש ברוך הוא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next topic on the memory list, לוט. Here it is the reverse of אברהם: almost all names are ordinary, with one holy exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לוט mostly speaks to the מלאכים, so those names are חול. In this פסוק, though, he goes on to thank the one who saved his life. Only ה׳ has power over life and death, so this אדני must be ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: To cause death and to give life
The Holy One, Blessed be He: ה׳

phrases.english: All names stated in connection with Lot are ordinary;
except for this one, which is holy,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיֹּאמֶר לוֹט אֲלֵהֶם, אַל נָא אֲדֹנָי,
phrases.english: as it says: "And Lot said to them: Please, not so, Adonai;
phrases.notes: בראשית 19:18–19.

phrases.aramaic: הִנֵּה נָא מָצָא עַבְדְּךָ חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ וְגוֹ׳״ –
phrases.english: behold, your servant has found favor in your eyes," and so on.
The One Who has the power to kill and to give life,
phrases.notes: The rest of the פסוק, hinted at by 'and so on', talks about saving לוט's life. That is the clue.

phrases.english: that is the Holy One, Blessed be He.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next topic from the memory list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the לוט story names are חול except 'אדני' in בראשית 19:18, which is קודש.

steps.title: נבות names are holy, מיכה names are ordinary
steps.stepSummary: The first opinion rules that all names in the נבות story are קודש, and all names in the מיכה story are חול.
steps.simpleTranslation: All names connected to נבות are holy; those connected to מיכה are ordinary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives two more topics from the memory list. In the נבות story the names mean ה׳; in the מיכה story they mean his idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the נבות story, the false witnesses said he cursed אלהים, meaning ה׳‎. מיכה made an idol, so this opinion says every אלהים in his story refers to that idol and is not holy.

keyTerms.meaning: The man killed through false testimony that he cursed ה׳ and the king
The man in שופטים who made an idol

phrases.english: All names stated in connection with Naboth are holy,
phrases.notes: מלכים א 21:13: 'נבות cursed אלהים and the king.'

phrases.english: those in connection with Micah are ordinary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of topics from step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Names in the נבות story are קודש; names in the מיכה story are חול.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר splits the מיכה names by spelling
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר agrees about נבות. For מיכה, he says names spelled with אלף-למד are חול and names spelled with יוד-הי are קודש, except 'בית האלהים בשילה', which is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: With נבות, holy. With מיכה, some are ordinary and some are holy. Those spelled with אלף-למד are ordinary; those spelled with יוד-הי are holy, except this one, which is spelled with אלף-למד and is holy: 'All the days that the house of אלהים was in שילה.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר disagrees with step 17 about מיכה. He gives a spelling rule, then one exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אלהים (אלף-למד) in the מיכה story refers to the idol, but ה׳'s main name (יוד-הי) can never mean an idol, so those are holy. The one exception is 'בית האלהים בשילה': it is spelled with אלף-למד, but it clearly means the משכן of ה׳ in שילה, so it is holy.

keyTerms.meaning: A name beginning with א-ל, like אֱלֹהִים
A name beginning with י-ה‎, ה׳'s main four-letter name
The place where the משכן stood

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume the word אלהים is always holy. Here the same spelling can mean an idol (חול) or ה׳‎ (קודש); context decides.
steps.whatToRemember: Whether a name is קודש depends on whom it refers to, not just how it looks. With אברהם and לוט the question is whether it means ה׳ or the guests. With מיכה, רבי אליעזר uses spelling plus context.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: In connection with Naboth, they are holy;

phrases.aramaic: בְּמִיכָה – יֵשׁ מֵהֶן חוֹל וְיֵשׁ מֵהֶן קֹדֶשׁ.
phrases.english: in connection with Micah, some of them are ordinary and some of them are holy.

phrases.aramaic: אָלֶף לָמֶד – חוֹל, יוֹד הֵי – קֹדֶשׁ;
phrases.english: Those spelled alef-lamed are ordinary; those spelled yod-heh are holy;
phrases.notes: Alef-lamed is the name אלהים. Yod-heh is ה׳'s main four-letter name.

phrases.aramaic: חוּץ מִזֶּה, שֶׁאָלֶף לָמֶד וְהוּא קֹדֶשׁ:
phrases.english: except for this one, which is alef-lamed and yet holy:
"All the days that the house of God was in Shiloh."
phrases.notes: שופטים 18:31.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with step 17's ruling about מיכה, while agreeing about נבות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With מיכה, אלף-למד names are חול and יוד-הי names are קודש, except 'בית האלהים בשילה', which is קודש.

steps.title: The Names in the Story of גבעת בנימין
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says the names in the גבעת בנימין story are חול. רבי יהושע says they are קודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the names in the story of גבעת בנימין: רבי אליעזר says they are ordinary, and רבי יהושע says they are holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new case in its list: the names used when the tribes asked whether to fight שבט בנימין. רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע disagree about them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whom the tribes were asking. If they asked ה׳, the names are holy. If not, the names are ordinary. This step only gives the two rulings, and the next steps explain the reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: Gibeah of Benjamin, the town where the war against שבט בנימין began

phrases.english: All the names stated in the story of Gibeah of Benjamin –
phrases.notes: This is the war story in שופטים 20.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: ordinary,
Rabbi Yehoshua says: holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list of stories, after נבות and מיכה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: the names are חול. רבי יהושע: the names are קודש.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר Asks: Would ה׳ Promise and Not Deliver?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר challenges רבי יהושע: if ה׳ answered them, why did they lose?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said to him: Does He promise and then not do it?!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר attacks רבי יהושע's view. If ה׳ told the tribes to go to war, how could they have been defeated?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tribes were told to go up, and they lost. רבי אליעזר argues that ה׳ never breaks a promise. So the one answering them could not have been ה׳, and the names must be חול.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it really be that...? (a word that opens a strong question)

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said to him:
Does He promise and not do it?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהושע's ruling from step 19
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע's view that the names are קודש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ה׳ keeps His promises. The tribes were promised and still lost, so it was not ה׳ answering.

steps.title: רבי יהושע Answers: They Never Asked If They Would Win
steps.stepSummary: ה׳ did what He promised. The tribes only asked whether to go, not whether they would win. When they finally asked about winning, ה׳ promised victory.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע said to him: What He promised, He did. But they did not check whether they would win or lose. At the end, when they did check, Heaven agreed with them, as the פסוק says: פנחס בן אלעזר בן אהרן stood before it in those days and said, Shall I go out again to war against my brother בנימין, or shall I stop?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע defends his view. ה׳ only answered the exact question they asked, and the first times they never asked if they would win.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer "go up" was true, but it was not a promise of victory. Only the last time did פנחס ask whether to go on or stop, and then ה׳ promised to give בנימין into their hands. So ה׳ never broke a promise, and the names can stay קודש.

keyTerms.meaning: They checked or tested (they asked about it)
Heaven agreed with them and approved their plan

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהושע does not say ה׳ failed to keep a promise. He says ה׳ never promised victory until the last time.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua said to him:
What He promised, He did;
but they did not check
whether to win or to be defeated.
At the last time, when they did check –
they agreed with them,
phrases.notes: He means that Heaven agreed and gave them a real promise of victory.

phrases.english: as it is said:
"And Pinchas son of Elazar son of Aharon (the Kohen)
phrases.notes: שופטים 20:28. Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, since the פסוק itself does not have it.

phrases.english: was standing before it in those days, saying:
Shall I yet again go out to war
with [the children of] Binyamin my brother,
or shall I stop, etc."
phrases.notes: The "etc." is the rest of the פסוק, where ה׳ says: Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אליעזר's challenge from step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the promise: the answer only covered the exact question asked
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "Go up" meant a promise of victory, so losing proves it was not ה׳.
steps.terutzMaskana: "Go up" was not a promise to win. Victory was promised only when they asked about it, and then they won.

steps.title: Every שלמה in שיר השירים Means ה׳, With One Exception
steps.stepSummary: Every שלמה in שיר השירים is holy and means ה׳, the One Who owns peace. The exception is "the thousand are yours, Shlomo," which refers to King שלמה himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Every "שלמה" mentioned in שיר השירים is holy: a song to the One to Whom peace belongs. Except for this one: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me; the thousand are for you, שלמה." That שלמה is the king himself, and "two hundred for those who guard its fruit" means the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new book, שיר השירים. It rules that the name שלמה there means ה׳, except in one פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The name שלמה is read like שלום, so it points to ה׳, the One Who owns peace. In "הָאֶלֶף לְךָ שְׁלֹמֹה" the פסוק is talking to the human king, and it gives the "guards of the fruit" a share. Those guards are the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: To the One Whom peace belongs to

phrases.english: Every "Shlomo" stated in Song of Songs –
is holy: a song to the One Whom peace belongs to;
phrases.notes: The name שלמה is being read like שלום, "peace."

phrases.english: except for this: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me;
the thousand are for you, Shlomo" –
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 8:12

phrases.english: that is Shlomo himself,
"and two hundred for those who guard its fruit" – the Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the list of names, moving to שיר השירים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every שלמה in שיר השירים is קודש, except "הָאֶלֶף לְךָ שְׁלֹמֹה," which refers to King שלמה.

steps.title: Some Say the Bed of שלמה Is Also Ordinary
steps.stepSummary: Another opinion adds a second exception: "הנה מטתו שלשלמה" also refers to King שלמה, so it is חול.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say that this one too is ordinary: "Behold the bed of Shlomo, sixty mighty men surround it."
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion, introduced with יש אומרים, agrees with the rule but adds one more exception.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that שלמה in שיר השירים is usually holy. On a first reading, the יש אומרים say the פסוק about the bed and its sixty guards is also talking about the human king, so this name is חול too. Steps 24–26 question this reading and end up changing it.
steps.whatToRemember: Whether a name is holy or ordinary depends on whom the פסוק is talking about. ה׳ means קודש, and a person or idol means חול. In שיר השירים, שלמה usually means ה׳. On a first reading the יש אומרים adds 'מטתו שלשלמה' as a second exception, but steps 24-26 reread it: the יש אומרים holds that 'האלף לך שלמה' is holy and only 'מטתו' is חול.

phrases.english: And some say: this one too is ordinary:
"Behold the bed of Shlomo; sixty."
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 3:7. The "sixty" are the sixty mighty men guarding the bed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second exception to the rule in step 22
steps.mimraCoreRuling: "הִנֵּה מִטָּתוֹ שֶׁלִּשְׁלֹמֹה" is also חול, because it refers to King שלמה.

steps.title: What does 'this too' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא checks how to read 'אף זה' in the יש אומרים: does it mean this verse is also חול, and the first one even more so?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'This too': does that mean this one is חול, and the other one obviously is?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what the words 'אף זה' in the יש אומרים (step 23) really mean. This sets up a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אף זה' sounds like 'this too is חול, on top of the first exception.' On that reading, both תנאים agree that 'the thousand are yours, Shlomo' means King שלמה. The גמרא wants to confirm this reading before it attacks it.

keyTerms.meaning: And it does not need to be said (the other case is even more obvious)

phrases.english: "This too" —
phrases.notes: These are the words of the יש אומרים from the last step, about 'הנה מטתו שלשלמה.'

phrases.english: and it is not even necessary to say that other one?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how to read the wording of the יש אומרים in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'אף זה' mean the יש אומרים agrees the first verse ('האלף לך שלמה') is also חול?

steps.title: שמואל's teaching fits neither opinion
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads 'the thousand are yours, Shlomo' as the Kingdom of Heaven, which is holy. On the simple reading, both opinions say that verse is חול.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said a kingdom that kills one out of six people is not punished. He learns it from the verse: the 'thousand' go to ה׳'s kingdom and the 'two hundred' to the earthly kingdom. So שמואל agrees with neither the first תנא nor the יש אומרים?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the simple reading of the יש אומרים, using a teaching of שמואל that treats 'Shlomo' in that verse as ה׳.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions in steps 22-23 call 'האלף לך שלמה' חול, meaning King שלמה. But שמואל reads that same 'שלמה' as the Kingdom of Heaven, which means it is קודש. A respected אמורא would not be left with no source, so something must be off.

phrases.english: But what about that which Shmuel said:
A kingdom that kills one out of six
in the world is not punished,
as it is said: "My vineyard, which is mine, is before me;
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 8:12

phrases.english: the thousand are yours, Shlomo" — this is for the Kingdom of Heaven,
"and two hundred for those who guard its fruit" —
this is for the earthly kingdom;
phrases.notes: 200 out of the total 1,200 is one sixth. That is where 'one out of six' comes from.

phrases.english: So Shmuel is not like the first opinion
and not like "some say"?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reading of 'אף זה' raised in step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of the יש אומרים, in which 'האלף לך שלמה' is חול
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל reads that 'Shlomo' as ה׳‎ (קודש). If both opinions call it חול, שמואל matches no תנא.

steps.title: Rereading the יש אומרים to fit שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The יש אומרים really says that 'the thousand' is holy and only 'his bed' is חול. שמואל follows that view.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what it means. Some say: 'the thousand' is holy, and only 'his bed' is חול. שמואל holds like this יש אומרים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing how we read the יש אומרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The יש אומרים does not add a second exception. It swaps the exception. 'האלף לך שלמה' becomes קודש, and 'מטתו שלשלמה' is the only חול one. That gives שמואל a תנא to rely on.
steps.whatToRemember: The first תנא says only 'האלף לך שלמה' is חול. The יש אומרים says only 'מטתו שלשלמה' is חול. שמואל follows the יש אומרים.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the יש אומרים as 'this too is חול.' After this answer, it means 'this one is holy, and that one is חול.'

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it is saying: And some say:
this one is holy;
phrases.notes: 'This one' is 'the thousand are yours, Shlomo.'

phrases.english: and that one is ordinary: the one about his bed.
And Shmuel said his teaching like "some say."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording of the opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The יש אומרים adds 'מטתו' as a second חול verse, so 'האלף' is חול for both opinions.
steps.terutzMaskana: The יש אומרים holds 'האלף' is קודש and only 'מטתו' is חול, and שמואל follows it.

steps.title: Kings in Daniel are ordinary except one
steps.stepSummary: Every 'king' in ספר דניאל is חול, except the verse 'You, O king, king of kings...', which is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the 'kings' mentioned in דניאל are חול, except this one, which is holy: 'You, O king, king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the last topic on its memory list (step 11): the word 'king' in ספר דניאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In דניאל, 'king' usually means a human king such as נבוכדנצר, so it is חול. One verse is singled out as קודש. This follows the same pattern as the שלמה rule in שיר השירים.

phrases.english: All the "kings" mentioned in Daniel are ordinary;
except for this one, which is holy:
"You, O king, king of kings,
phrases.notes: דניאל 2:37. The word in square brackets is the corrected wording.

phrases.english: to whom the God of heaven

phrases.aramaic: מַלְכוּתָא חִסְנָא וְתׇקְפָּא וִיקָרָא יְהַב לָךְ״.
phrases.english: has given you the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from שיר השירים to a new list about ספר דניאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All 'kings' in דניאל are חול except 'אנת מלכא מלך מלכיא...', which is קודש.

steps.title: A second holy verse in Daniel
steps.stepSummary: The יש אומרים adds the verse 'My lord, the dream is for your enemy' as holy as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say this one is also holy, as it says: 'My lord, the dream is for your enemy, and its meaning for your foe.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion adds another exception, so one more verse in דניאל is holy. The reason comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word under discussion here is 'מרי' ('my lord'). On the simple reading דניאל is speaking to נבוכדנצר. The יש אומרים says 'my lord' here means ה׳.

phrases.english: And some say: this one too is holy —
as it is said: "My lord, the dream is for your enemy
phrases.notes: דניאל 4:16

phrases.english: and its meaning for your foe" —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second holy exception to the list in step 27.

steps.title: Daniel would not curse Israel
steps.stepSummary: If 'my lord' meant נבוכדנצר, his enemies would be Israel, and דניאל would be cursing Israel. That cannot be.
steps.simpleTranslation: To whom is he saying this? If you think he is saying it to נבוכדנצר, who are his enemies? Israel. Would דניאל be cursing Israel?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves the יש אומרים by showing the simple reading leads to an impossible result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Let the dream fall on your enemies' is a curse on the listener's enemies. נבוכדנצר's enemies were the Jewish people, and דניאל would never curse them. So 'my lord' must be speaking to ה׳, and the word is holy.

keyTerms.meaning: To whom is he saying it?

steps.whatToRemember: In דניאל, 'king' is usually חול, except 'אנת מלכא מלך מלכיא.' The יש אומרים also counts 'מרי חלמא לשנאך' as holy, because דניאל would never curse Israel.

phrases.english: To whom is he saying this?

phrases.aramaic: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ לִנְבוּכַדְ נֶצַּר קָאָמַר לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: If you think he is saying it to Nebuchadnezzar,
who are his enemies? Israel;
would he be cursing Israel?!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאן קָאָמַר? אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ לִנְבוּכַדְ נֶצַּר קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the יש אומרים in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: That 'מרי' in 'מרי חלמא לשנאך' refers to ה׳ and is קודש
steps.raayaSupportSource: Reading it as נבוכדנצר would make דניאל curse Israel, which is impossible.

steps.title: The תנא קמא Can Explain the Verse Too
steps.stepSummary: The proof from step 29 is pushed away. The תנא קמא can say that נבוכדנצר also had non-Jewish enemies, and those are the ones דניאל cursed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And does the תנא קמא think that נבוכדנצר only had Jewish enemies and no non-Jewish enemies?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the תנא קמא against the argument that he makes דניאל curse Israel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 said that if 'my lord' meant נבוכדנצר, 'your enemy' would have to mean Israel. The גמרא answers that נבוכדנצר had plenty of non-Jewish enemies too. So the תנא קמא can read the verse as חול with no problem.

keyTerms.meaning: The first opinion in a teaching, the one stated before the יש אומרים

phrases.english: And does the first tanna hold:
There are enemies who are Israel,
but there are no enemies who are gentiles?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 29 against the תנא קמא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The argument that the תנא קמא's reading makes דניאל curse Israel.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument assumed נבוכדנצר's only enemies were Israel. He also had non-Jewish enemies.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: Substitute Names Count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: an oath with any כנוי of ה׳ makes the witnesses liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he made them swear with any of the substitute names of ה׳, they are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes a new line. This sets up the next step, where a contradiction is raised against it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules that witnesses are liable for a false שבועת העדות even if the oath did not use the actual name of ה׳. A כנוי, a title used for ה׳, is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Substitute names or titles for ה׳, not His actual name
Liable, here for a false שבועת העדות
Etc., meaning the quote continues in the משנה

phrases.english: And with any of the substitute names –
phrases.notes: These are titles that describe ה׳, used in place of His actual name.

phrases.english: these are liable, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side discussion about ספר דניאל and returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath with a כנוי of ה׳ is enough to make the witnesses liable.

steps.title: A ברייתא Says the Oath Must Use the Name
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא compares the word אלה in סוטה and in שבועת העדות. It concludes that the witnesses' oath must be with the actual Name, which goes against the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא asks why the Torah says 'ה׳ shall make you a curse and an oath' when it already said the כהן makes the סוטה swear with an oath of curse. It answers that the extra words teach about witnesses. Witnesses' oath is also called אלה. So just as the סוטה's אלה is an oath with the Name, the witnesses' אלה must also be an oath with the Name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the shared word אלה to connect סוטה with שבועת העדות. The סוטה's oath uses ה׳'s name, so the witnesses' oath must too. That would mean a כנוי is not enough, which goes against the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: And they raised a contradiction between two sources
A curse, here an oath that carries a curse
Why does the verse need to say this?
There, meaning in the other passage

steps.confusionAlert: 'Here' (כאן) means the witnesses' oath in ויקרא. 'There' (להלן) means the סוטה. The rule is learned from the סוטה and applied to the witnesses.

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
"ה׳ shall make you a curse and an oath" –
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:21

phrases.english: Why does the verse need to say this?
Wasn't it already said:
"And the priest shall make the woman swear
with the oath of the curse"!
Because it says: "And he heard the voice of an אלה" –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

phrases.english: "אלה" is said here
and "אלה" is said there;
just as there it is an oath,
so too here it is an oath;
just as there it is with the Name,
so too here it is with the Name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה quoted in step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a כנוי is enough for a שבועת העדות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא learns from the shared word אלה that the witnesses' oath must be with the Name, just like the סוטה's oath. So a כנוי should not be enough.

steps.title: אביי: Two Different Opinions
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the sources do not clash. The ברייתא follows רבי חנינא בר אידי, and the משנה follows the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: There is no difficulty. The ברייתא is the view of רבי חנינא בר אידי, and the משנה is the view of the רבנן.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction by saying each source follows a different תנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי does not try to make the ברייתא and the משנה agree. He says they reflect a real argument. רבי חנינא בר אידי requires the actual Name, and the רבנן of the משנה accept a כנוי.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult, meaning there is no real contradiction

phrases.english: Abaye said: It is not difficult;
this is Rabbi Chanina bar Idi,
phrases.notes: 'This' means the ברייתא that requires the Name.

phrases.english: that is the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning each source to a different תנא (the sources reflect a real argument).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and the משנה seemed to be stating one rule and contradicting each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבי חנינא בר אידי, who requires the Name. The משנה follows the רבנן, who accept a כנוי.

steps.title: רבי חנינא בר אידי's Source
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי חנינא בר אידי requires the Name. Just as the Torah's commands to swear and to curse use the Name, so do its prohibitions.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: רבי חנינא בר אידי says, since the Torah says 'swear' and 'do not swear,' and 'curse' and 'do not curse': just as 'swear' is with the Name, so is 'do not swear.' And just as 'curse' is with the Name, so is 'do not curse.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that רבי חנינא בר אידי really holds that the Name is required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא בר אידי pairs each command with its matching prohibition. The command to swear or curse is with the Name, so the prohibition must also be about swearing or cursing with the Name. This backs up אביי's claim that he is the one who requires the Name.
steps.whatToRemember: משנה (רבנן): a שבועת העדות with a כנוי makes the witnesses liable. רבי חנינא בר אידי: oaths and curses in the Torah must be with the actual Name.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אִידִי אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: As it was taught: Rabbi Chanina bar Idi says:
Since the Torah said
"swear" and "do not swear,"
"curse" and "do not curse" –
just as "swear" is with the Name,
so too "do not swear" is with the Name;
just as "curse" is with the Name,
so too "do not curse" is with the Name.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר אִידִי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports אביי's answer by showing רבי חנינא בר אידי's own view.
steps.raayaObject: אביי's claim that רבי חנינא בר אידי requires the Name.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי חנינא בר אידי pairs the Torah's commands to swear and curse with its prohibitions, all with the Name.

steps.title: A two-sided challenge to the Rabbis
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the רבנן. If they learn the גזירה שוה, they should require שם המיוחד. If they don't, they have no source that אלה means an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן: if they learn the גזירה שוה, let them require the special Name! If they don't learn the גזירה שוה, how do they know that the אלה here means an oath?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the רבנן. In step 33 אביי named them as the source of the משנה's rule that any כנוי is enough. It traps them between two options, and both seem to cause a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא in step 32 used the גזירה שוה from סוטה to require the Name. The סוטה's oath is with ה׳'s special name, so if the רבנן accept that גזירה שוה, they should require שם המיוחד, not accept a כנוי. If they reject it, they lose their source that the word אלה in the witnesses' verse means an oath at all.

keyTerms.meaning: They learn (they accept a tradition or derivation)
A comparison between two פסוקים that share the same word
The special, actual Name of ה׳
A curse; the word used in the פסוק about the witnesses
From where do they know it?

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: if they learn the גזירה שוה,
let us require the special Name!
If they do not learn the גזירה שוה,
from where do they know that 'אלה' means an oath?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After proving רבי חנינא בר אידי's view, the גמרא now questions how the רבנן handle the same source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The רבנן's position that a כנוי is enough for the witnesses' oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: accepting the גזירה שוה forces the Name, and rejecting it removes the source that אלה means an oath.

steps.title: The Rabbis learn the meaning of the word from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn from a ברייתא that אלה is a word for an oath, and the ברייתא brings support from the סוטה verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: They learn it from a ברייתא: 'An אלה' means nothing other than an oath. So it says: 'And the כהן shall make the woman swear with the oath of the curse.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן do not need the full גזירה שוה. A ברייתא simply teaches that the word אלה means an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סוטה verse is used here only to show how the word אלה is used in the Torah. It is not a full גזירה שוה that brings over every law of סוטה. So the רבנן get the meaning 'oath' without being forced to require the actual Name.

phrases.english: They derive it from what was taught in a ברייתא:
'An אלה':
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:1

phrases.english: 'אלה' is nothing other than a word for an oath,
and so it says:
'And the כהן shall make the woman swear
with the oath of the curse.'
phrases.notes: במדבר 5:21

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the second side of the dilemma in step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate source: a word-meaning teaching instead of a full גזירה שוה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the גזירה שוה, the רבנן have no source that אלה means an oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: A ברייתא teaches that אלה means an oath. This does not bring over the requirement of the Name.

steps.title: The סוטה verse says more than just אלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the סוטה verse says 'oath of the אלה.' That suggests אלה by itself is not an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there it is written 'the oath of the אלה'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof just brought. The verse in סוטה adds the word 'oath' next to אלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If אלה already meant an oath, the Torah would not need to say 'oath of the אלה.' The extra word seems to show that אלה alone means a curse, not an oath. If so, the verse cannot prove what the ברייתא wanted.

phrases.english: There, 'the oath of the אלה' is written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof from the ברייתא in step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that אלה means an oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The verse pairs אלה with the word 'oath,' which implies the two words are not the same thing.

steps.title: The ברייתא means an אלה always comes with an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: an אלה is only spoken together with an oath, as the סוטה verse shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: 'An אלה' is only together with an oath. So it says: 'And the כהן shall make the woman swear with the oath of the curse.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by explaining the ברייתא differently. It does not say אלה means oath. It says an אלה always goes together with an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's wording changes from 'a word for an oath' to 'only with an oath.' Now the סוטה verse is a good proof, because it shows the two words appearing together. So wherever the Torah mentions an אלה, as with the witnesses, an oath is included too.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he is saying (a rereading)

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן do not take the full גזירה שוה from סוטה, so they do not require the actual Name. They only learn that an אלה always comes with an oath, which shows that the witnesses' אלה includes an oath.
steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is quoted twice with almost the same words. The one change is from לְשׁוֹן שְׁבוּעָה (a word meaning oath) to בִּשְׁבוּעָה (together with an oath). That small change is the whole answer.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
'An אלה':
'אלה' comes only together with an oath,
and so it says:
'And the כהן shall make the woman swear
with the oath of the curse.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 37 by rereading the ברייתא from step 36.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was claiming that the word אלה itself means an oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means that an אלה is always joined with an oath, and the סוטה verse shows that pairing.
